title: Flexor Tendon Zones, Pulley System, Repair and Rehabilitation

steps.say: The flexor system is dividing into five zones, and the zone is dictating prognosis. Zone one is lying beyond the FDS insertion, zone two is running from the A1 pulley to the FDS insertion as no mans land, zone three is crossing the palm, zone four is passing the carpal tunnel, and zone five is lying in the forearm.
steps.tx: **Flexor tendon** zones (the five surgical territories of the finger flexors) divide the system into **five** regions: **Zone I** distal to **FDS** insertion (superficialis attachment near the fingertip), **Zone II** from **A1 pulley** to FDS insertion, the **no mans land** (the tight fibro-osseous segment with the worst results), **Zone III** palm, **Zone IV** carpal tunnel, and **Zone V** forearm.

vis.caption: Tendon zones I to V with FDP, FDS, and the A1 and A2 pulleys; zone II is no mans land. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Pulleys are holding the tendon against bone, and two of them are untouchable. Five annular pulleys from A1 to A5 and three cruciform pulleys from C1 to C3 are forming the sheath. The A2 and A4 pulleys are essential because their loss is letting the tendon bowstring.
steps.tx: The digital annular **pulley** system (fibrous rings holding flexors to bone) consists of **five** annular pulleys **A1** to A5 and **three** cruciform pulleys **C1** to C3, with the **A2** and **A4** pulleys essential to prevent **bowstringing** (tendon lifting off bone and losing its moment arm). Sheath surgery preserves A2 and A4 above all.

Three: C1 to C3 collapsible cross bands
A2 and A4, the bowstring preventers

steps.say: Tendons are eating through blood vessels and bathwater both. Longitudinal vincula brevia and longa are perfusing segments directly while synovial fluid is diffusing nutrients into the rest. Repairs are preserving both routes and are leaving the gliding surface glassy smooth.
steps.tx: Tendon **nutrition** (how relatively avascular tendon stays alive) is mediated by both direct vascular perfusion via longitudinal **vincula** brevia and longa (small mesentery vessels) and passive **synovial fluid diffusion** (nutrient bath inside the sheath). Repair handling spares the vincula and the sheath lining, since a stripped tendon starves and sticks.

rows: Spare vincula and the gliding surface

steps.tx: Strength comes from strands: **4-strand** and **6-strand** cores built as a **modified Kessler** locking loop, a **cruciate** cross, or a **Strickland** braid, all tied in **3-0** or **4-0** **braided** or monofilament thread. Each extra strand crossing the gap is raising the failure load.
steps.say: Several strands are now crossing every repair. Four-strand and six-strand cores such as modified Kessler, cruciate, and Strickland patterns are replacing the old two-strand stitch. Three-oh or four-oh braided suture is carrying the load.

A fine outer loop is finishing every core repair. A continuous running epitendinous suture in five-oh or six-oh material is tidying the edge and is smoothing glide through the pulleys. It is adding twenty to fifty percent more strength, so skipping it is leaving a catching weaker tendon.
steps.tx: Core tendon suture must be paired with a continuous running **epitendinous suture** (a fine peripheral loop burying the repair edge) in **5-0** or **6-0** material to smooth tendon **gliding** (frictionless slide through the sheath) and increase repair tensile strength by **20%** to **50%**. The outer loop shares load and prevents edge catch.

steps.say: Repaired tendons are moving within days, not weeks. Early active motion protocols such as Manchester and Saint John are starting controlled glide within three to five days of repair. Movement is preventing the restrictive peritendinous adhesions that are freezing still tendons.
steps.tx: **Early active motion** protocols (controlled postoperative glide programmes) such as Manchester or Saint John protocols, initiated within **3** to **5 days** post-repair, prevent restrictive **peritendinous adhesion** (scar tethering tendon to sheath) formation. A moved tendon glides; an immobilised one glues itself down.

steps.say: A grabbed jersey is tearing the deep flexor off the bone. Jersey finger is avulsing the flexor digitorum profundus from the distal phalanx base when the grip is forcibly extended. The ring finger is suffering this in seventy five percent of cases because it is protruding furthest.
steps.tx: **Jersey finger** (closed FDP avulsion when a caught finger is forcibly extended) is avulsion of the **flexor digitorum profundus** **FDP** tendon (the deep thumb-side-out flexor) from the **distal phalanx** base (the fingertip bone insertion), most commonly affecting the **ring finger** in **75%** of cases. The player cannot bend the fingertip, though the palm-side middle joint still flexes.

right.title: Types II and III

steps.tx: **Leddy and Pack** classification (the Jersey finger grading) sorts retraction depth: **Type I** retracts into the **palm** with disrupted **vincula** (blood supply torn, repair within days), **Type II** stalls at the **PIP** joint (middle knuckle), and **Type III** carries a **bony avulsion** (a bone chip off the insertion) trapped at **A4**. The chip blocks reduction until it is freed.
steps.say: Retraction depth is grading Jersey injuries. Type one is pulling back into the palm with torn vincula and is needing repair within days. Type two is stalling at the PIP joint. Type three is carrying a bony chip jammed at A4 that is blocking reduction.
